sections.html:
Up in the Ozarks of northwest Arkansas, Washington County has Fayetteville as its seat and its biggest city. It counted 245,871 residents in 2020, and 271,213 are estimated for 2025.

Thirteen incorporated places lie inside the county: Elkins, Elm Springs, Farmington, Fayetteville, Goshen, Greenland, Johnson, Lincoln, Prairie Grove, Springdale, Tontitown, West Fork and Winslow. Two of them, Elm Springs and Springdale, also extend into Benton County. A homeowner in either city should learn which county bills the parcel before phoning an assessor or collector.

The ground itself can affect value. Karst country brings springs, sinkholes and caves, and the Boone Formation limestone under the Springfield Plateau is known for solution and collapse sinkholes. Buyers will ask a seller about any sinkhole or settling foundation.

Property tax here is split among three county offices. One values property, one books Equalization Board appointments, and one mails bills and takes money. A fourth, the Treasurer, is a separate office connected to the Collector.

OfficeWhat it doesPhone and hours
AssessorValues real and personal property, hears informal appealsAppraiser, 479-444-1500, weekdays 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.
County ClerkSchedules Equalization Board hearings479-444-1711
CollectorMails statements, collects tax479-444-1526 if no statement by April 15

Look up your parcel for free on the Assessor's site, and pull receipts through Search Tax Records on the Collector's. Online payment takes a credit card only and adds a processing fee, while mail and in-person payment are also open.

sections.h2: How the county values a house
sections.html:
A house is valued at market value, the price it would likely bring in an arm's-length sale. Genuine farmland is valued by its use. Homes with similar traits are grouped into neighborhoods and valued together, which is mass appraisal. Act 139 of 2023 requires counties to reappraise market-value real estate every four years, and this county's cycle started in 2023.

New construction is added to the rolls yearly. Owners should report it, and permitted work inside a city gets a field inspection. A garage, a finished basement or an extra room built before you sell will change the value at the next assessment.

School districts and elected county and city officials set the rates every year. The Collector's page describes the bill as roughly 1 percent of the value of your home, car and other property, which is only a rough guide. For the current assessment ratio and millage rate, call the Assessor.

An owner's primary residence qualifies for a homestead credit worth up to $600 off the bill. To claim it, notify the Assessor in the county where you live.

  • A reappraisal cannot push taxable value up more than 5 percent a year on a primary residence, or more than 10 percent on vacant and commercial property.
  • Taxable value cannot go up from reappraisal for owners who are 65 or older or who are disabled under Social Security standards.
  • Seniors and disabled owners show a driver's license or state ID, or proof of disability.
  • A home held in a trust, or one where the occupant lives in a nursing home, can still qualify.
  • Mobile and modular homes count as real estate and are eligible.

The credit does not follow the house automatically. A buyer who plans to live there should visit the Assessor's office after closing to claim it.

October 15 is the due date for real estate and personal property tax. Assessing runs from January 1 through May 31. Because Arkansas bills in arrears, the October payment reflects an assessment made earlier in the year.

Pay real estate late and you owe a 10 percent penalty plus 10 percent annual interest. Late personal property takes the 10 percent penalty. If personal property is assessed after May 31, a 10 percent late assessment fee applies, though newly bought property can be assessed within 30 days of purchase without it.

Real estate left unpaid can be sent to the Commissioner of State Lands for collection. If you have fallen behind, call the Collector.

A sale that closes mid-year raises a question: who pays a bill not yet issued? Ask the title company how it plans to handle it, and put the answer in the contract. A written line stating who pays removes any doubt at the closing table.

Call the appraiser at 479-444-1500 first, on or before the third Monday in August. If that does not settle it, book an Equalization Board hearing through the County Clerk by the same date. The board meets from August 1 through September 30, and a decision can be taken on to County Court and then Circuit Court.

The appeal calendar repeats every year and leaves little slack:

  • July: the Assessor sends notices and the Clerk begins scheduling appointments.
  • August 1: the board holds its first meeting.
  • Third Monday in August: the last day to schedule a hearing.
  • September 30: the last day for regular meetings.

Take comparable sales, repair estimates and photos of the problem with you. A house under contract cannot wait past these dates, so start before you list.

sections.h2: Before you list a Washington County house
sections.html:
A short checklist keeps the tax side of a sale from becoming a surprise.

  1. Look up the parcel on the Assessor's site and confirm that the owner name, size and improvements match what you own.
  2. Check the Collector's records for the current bill and past receipts.
  3. Confirm that the homestead credit is on the house, since a missing credit makes the bill higher than a buyer expects.
  4. Ask whether any part of the property is classed as farmland, vacant land or personal property such as a mobile home.
  5. Decide whether to challenge a value now or let the buyer deal with it after closing.

If the Assessor's record is wrong, fixing it before a buyer's title company finds the error saves back and forth later.

Every deed in Arkansas carries a real property transfer tax of $3.30 for each $1,000 of consideration, and the contract should say who pays. The state's Miscellaneous Tax Section sells the transfer stamps and answers questions at 501-682-7187.

Back taxes, needed repairs or a tenant in place can make an ordinary listing difficult, and a cash sale can ease each of those. Cash Home Buyers purchases houses as-is, and we explain what the title company will pay from your proceeds before you decide. We promise no price until we have reviewed the property.

Whenever taxes are owed, get the balance from the Collector before anything else. The title company can settle it out of the proceeds at closing, which gives the buyer a clean title. File the paid receipt with your closing papers.

faqs.q: When are Washington County, Arkansas property taxes due?
faqs.a: Every October 15. Real estate paid later takes a 10 percent penalty and gathers 10 percent annual interest.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Washington County assessment?
faqs.a: Begin with the appraiser at 479-444-1500, then book an Equalization Board hearing through the County Clerk at 479-444-1711. Both steps must be done by the third Monday in August.

faqs.q: What is the homestead credit in Washington County?
faqs.a: Up to $600 off the bill on your primary residence, claimed by notifying the Assessor.

faqs.q: Is there a limit on how much my assessment can rise?
faqs.a: Yes. Reappraisal can lift taxable value no more than 5 percent a year on a primary residence, and owners 65 or older or disabled see no reappraisal increase.

faqs.q: Who do I call if I did not get my tax statement?
faqs.a: Phone the Collector at 479-444-1526 if no statement arrives by April 15.
